claim: A 6 day viability screen using 94 drugs was performed on 15 MM cell lines that had been characterised using whole-exome sequencing, copy number analysis and gene expression arrays.
source: A 6 day viability screen using 94 drugs including small molecule inhibitors and cytotoxic chemotherapeutics (Supplementary file 1) was performed on 15 MM cell lines (Supplementary file 2) that had been characterised using whole-exome sequencing, copy number analysis and gene expression arrays.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design of the drug screen, including the number of drugs, cell lines, and characterization methods used.

claim: The screen generated 1425 single agent activity data profiles across the 15 cell lines.
source: We generated 1425 single agent activity data profiles across the 15 cell lines (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript states the number of data profiles generated and references Figure 1A showing the results.

claim: There were 24 significant associations (false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.2) between single agent response and the presence of a genomic alteration.
source: There were 24 significant associations (false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.2) between single agent response and the presence of a genomic alteration.
evidence: The manuscript reports the statistical analysis results identifying significant associations.

claim: The most statistically significant sensitising association was between BAP1 LOF mutations and treatment with recombinant TRAIL (FDR = 0.18, effect size −0.48).
source: The most statistically significant sensitising association seen was between BAP1 LOF mutations (mt BAP1) and treatment with recombinant TRAIL (rTRAIL; FDR = 0.18, effect size −0.48) (Figure 1B,C and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical measures (FDR and effect size) for the BAP1-TRAIL association and references supporting figures.

claim: No significant effect on cell viability was observed in BAP1 wild-type lines when treated with rTRAIL.
source: No significant effect on cell viability was observed in BAP1 wild-type (wt BAP1) lines when treated with rTRAIL.
evidence: The manuscript states the observation from the experimental data.

claim: 6 of the 8 cell lines (75%) harbouring a BAP1 LOF mutation were sensitive or partially sensitive to a dose range of rTRAIL.
source: Strikingly, 6 of the 8 cell lines (75%) harbouring a BAP1 LOF mutation were sensitive or partially sensitive to a dose range of rTRAIL while 7 of the 9 cell lines (78%) harbouring wild-type BAP1 were resistant.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on the proportion of BAP1-mutant cell lines sensitive to rTRAIL.

claim: 7 of the 9 cell lines (78%) harbouring wild-type BAP1 were resistant to rTRAIL.
source: Strikingly, 6 of the 8 cell lines (75%) harbouring a BAP1 LOF mutation were sensitive or partially sensitive to a dose range of rTRAIL while 7 of the 9 cell lines (78%) harbouring wild-type BAP1 were resistant.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on the proportion of BAP1-wild-type cell lines resistant to rTRAIL.

claim: BAP1 LOF mutations correlated with a loss of BAP1 protein expression in the majority of cell lines.
source: BAP1 LOF mutations correlated with a loss of BAP1 protein expression in the majority of cell lines (Figure 1E).
evidence: The manuscript states the correlation and references Figure 1E showing immunoblot data.

claim: No sensitising association with BAP1 was observed for pemetrexed or cisplatin.
source: No sensitising association with BAP1 was observed for pemetrexed or cisplatin, which are current first line agents for the treatment of MM (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of association for these drugs and references supporting figures.

claim: Loss of BAP1 expression has been identified in uveal melanoma (47%).
source: Loss of BAP1 expression has also been identified in several other tumour types including uveal melanoma (47%) (Harbour et al., 2010), clear cell renal carcinoma (CCRC) (14%) (Peña-Llopis et al., 2012) and cholangiocarcinoma (7%) (Fujimoto et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature reporting BAP1 loss in uveal melanoma.

claim: Loss of BAP1 expression has been identified in clear cell renal carcinoma (14%).
source: Loss of BAP1 expression has also been identified in several other tumour types including uveal melanoma (47%) (Harbour et al., 2010), clear cell renal carcinoma (CCRC) (14%) (Peña-Llopis et al., 2012) and cholangiocarcinoma (7%) (Fujimoto et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature reporting BAP1 loss in clear cell renal carcinoma.

claim: Loss of BAP1 expression has been identified in cholangiocarcinoma (7%).
source: Loss of BAP1 expression has also been identified in several other tumour types including uveal melanoma (47%) (Harbour et al., 2010), clear cell renal carcinoma (CCRC) (14%) (Peña-Llopis et al., 2012) and cholangiocarcinoma (7%) (Fujimoto et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature reporting BAP1 loss in cholangiocarcinoma.

claim: Knockdown of BAP1 in two CCRC lines resulted in increased sensitivity to rTRAIL.
source: Notably, knockdown of BAP1 in two CCRC lines resulted in increased sensitivity to rTRAIL in addition to the MDAMB-231 breast cancer line (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results of BAP1 knockdown in CCRC lines and references supporting figures.

claim: Knockdown of BAP1 in the MDAMB-231 breast cancer line resulted in increased sensitivity to rTRAIL.
source: Notably, knockdown of BAP1 in two CCRC lines resulted in increased sensitivity to rTRAIL in addition to the MDAMB-231 breast cancer line (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results of BAP1 knockdown in breast cancer line and references supporting figures.

claim: Nine additional non-mesothelioma cell lines harbouring truncating mutations in BAP1 were identified in a panel of 1001 cancer cell lines.
source: We also analysed a panel of 1001 cancer cell lines submitted for whole exome and copy number analysis as part of the COSMIC cell lines project (Forbes et al., 2015) and identified nine additional non-mesothelioma cell lines harbouring truncating mutations in BAP1 (http://cancer.sanger.ac.uk/cancergenome/projects/cell_lines/).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of COSMIC database identifying BAP1-mutant cell lines.

claim: Treatment of cancer cell lines harbouring nonsense mutations in BAP1 with rTRAIL resulted in markedly reduced cell viability compared with cancer cell lines harbouring missense mutations.
source: Treatment of cancer cell lines harbouring nonsense mutations in BAP1 with rTRAIL resulted in markedly reduced cell viability compared with cancer cell lines harbouring missense mutations (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results comparing different types of BAP1 mutations and references supporting figure.

claim: rTRAIL sensitivity of the parental BAP1-null H226 MM line was significantly diminished following expression of wild-type BAP1.
source: rTRAIL sensitivity of the parental BAP1-null H226 MM line was significantly diminished following expression of wild-type BAP1 and each of the mutant constructs except those with an inactive deubiquitinating or ASXL protein-binding site (Figure 2C), implicating the function of these sites in BAP1-induced TRAIL resistance.
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results of BAP1 rescue experiments and references supporting figure.

claim: rTRAIL sensitivity was maintained in H226 cells expressing BAP1 with an inactive deubiquitinating site.
source: rTRAIL sensitivity of the parental BAP1-null H226 MM line was significantly diminished following expression of wild-type BAP1 and each of the mutant constructs except those with an inactive deubiquitinating or ASXL protein-binding site (Figure 2C), implicating the function of these sites in BAP1-induced TRAIL resistance.
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results showing that the C91A mutant did not rescue TRAIL resistance and references supporting figure.

claim: rTRAIL sensitivity was maintained in H226 cells expressing BAP1 with an inactive ASXL protein-binding site.
source: rTRAIL sensitivity of the parental BAP1-null H226 MM line was significantly diminished following expression of wild-type BAP1 and each of the mutant constructs except those with an inactive deubiquitinating or ASXL protein-binding site (Figure 2C), implicating the function of these sites in BAP1-induced TRAIL resistance.
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results showing that the ΔASXL mutant did not rescue TRAIL resistance and references supporting figure.

claim: The BAP1 deubiquitinase and ASXL-binding sites are key to the function of the PR-DUB.
source: The BAP1 deubiquitinase and ASXL-binding sites are key to the function of the PR-DUB, an epigenetic transcriptional regulatory complex composed of BAP1 and ASXL1.
evidence: The manuscript states the functional importance of these sites based on known biology of PR-DUB.

claim: Deubiquitination of H2AK119Ub alters chromatin architecture to modulate gene transcription.
source: Deubiquitination of the main substrate of the PR-DUB, H2AK119Ub, alters chromatin architecture to modulate gene transcription (Scheuermann et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature describing the mechanism of PR-DUB function.

claim: shRNA silencing of ASXL1 induced sensitivity to MEDI3039 and rTRAIL in the BAP1/ASXL1/ASXL2-wild-type MM line MPP-89.
source: Consistent with this shRNA silencing of ASXL1, but not ASXL2, induced sensitivity to MEDI3039 and rTRAIL in the BAP1/ASXL1/ASXL2-wild-type MM line MPP-89 (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results of ASXL1 knockdown and references supporting figures.

claim: shRNA silencing of ASXL2 did not induce sensitivity to MEDI3039 and rTRAIL in the BAP1/ASXL1/ASXL2-wild-type MM line MPP-89.
source: Consistent with this shRNA silencing of ASXL1, but not ASXL2, induced sensitivity to MEDI3039 and rTRAIL in the BAP1/ASXL1/ASXL2-wild-type MM line MPP-89 (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results of ASXL2 knockdown showing no effect and references supporting figures.

claim: H2AK119Ub expression was unaltered in the rTRAIL-sensitive H226 cells transduced with mutant constructs that disrupt PR-DUB activity.
source: Furthermore, H2AK119Ub expression was unaltered in the rTRAIL-sensitive H226 cells transduced with mutant constructs that disrupt PR-DUB activity, while the rTRAIL-resistant H226 cells transduced with a wild-type BAP1 construct exhibited lower H2AK119Ub levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results measuring H2AK119Ub levels and references supporting figure.

claim: rTRAIL-resistant H226 cells transduced with a wild-type BAP1 construct exhibited lower H2AK119Ub levels.
source: Furthermore, H2AK119Ub expression was unaltered in the rTRAIL-sensitive H226 cells transduced with mutant constructs that disrupt PR-DUB activity, while the rTRAIL-resistant H226 cells transduced with a wild-type BAP1 construct exhibited lower H2AK119Ub levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results measuring H2AK119Ub levels and references supporting figure.

claim: Among pathways significantly altered when comparing wild-type versus C91A BAP1 (FDR < 0.2) was that of apoptosis.
source: Among those pathways significantly altered when comparing wild-type versus C91A BAP1 (FDR < 0.2) was that of apoptosis.
evidence: The manuscript reports results of pathway analysis comparing gene expression between wild-type and mutant BAP1.

claim: There was altered mRNA expression of components of the extrinsic death pathway when comparing wild-type versus C91A BAP1.
source: In particular, there was altered mRNA expression of components of the extrinsic death pathway (Figure 2F and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The manuscript describes gene expression analysis results and references supporting figure.

claim: There were significantly decreased levels of the anti-apoptotic cIAP1/2 (p=2.32E-10) in the rTRAIL sensitive C91A BAP1-transduced cells relative to the rTRAIL resistant BAP1-wild-type transduced cells.
source: This manifested as an imbalance in levels of pro- and anti-apoptotic mRNA expression with, for example, significantly decreased levels of the anti-apoptotic cIAP1/2 (p=2.32E-10) and increased levels of the pro-apoptotic death receptor 5 (p=7.79E-10) in the rTRAIL sensitive C91A BAP1-transduced cells relative to the rTRAIL resistant BAP1-wild-type transduced cells.
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical analysis of gene expression differences with p-values.

claim: There were increased levels of the pro-apoptotic death receptor 5 (p=7.79E-10) in the rTRAIL sensitive C91A BAP1-transduced cells relative to the rTRAIL resistant BAP1-wild-type transduced cells.
source: This manifested as an imbalance in levels of pro- and anti-apoptotic mRNA expression with, for example, significantly decreased levels of the anti-apoptotic cIAP1/2 (p=2.32E-10) and increased levels of the pro-apoptotic death receptor 5 (p=7.79E-10) in the rTRAIL sensitive C91A BAP1-transduced cells relative to the rTRAIL resistant BAP1-wild-type transduced cells.
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical analysis of gene expression differences with p-values.

claim: Immunoblot analysis confirmed reduced protein expression of cIAP1/2 and c-FLIP in both C91A and ΔASXL BAP1-transduced cells relative to BAP1-wild-type transduced cells.
source: Immunoblot analysis confirmed reduced protein expression of cIAP1/2 and c-FLIP in both C91A and ΔASXL BAP1-transduced cells relative to BAP1-wild-type transduced cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: The manuscript describes immunoblot results confirming protein expression changes and references supporting figure.

claim: Flow cytometry analysis confirmed reduced DR4 and DR5 expression in C91A BAP1 transduced relative to BAP1-wild-type-transduced cells.
source: Flow cytometry analysis confirmed reduced DR4 and DR5 expression in C91A BAP1 transduced relative to BAP1-wild-type-transduced cells.
evidence: The manuscript describes flow cytometry results measuring death receptor expression.

claim: Knockdown of BAP1 in the BAP1 wild-type H2818 line resulted in a significant increase in DR4 expression only.
source: Knockdown of BAP1 in the BAP1 wild-type H2818 line resulted in a significant increase in DR4 expression only (Figure 2H).
evidence: The manuscript describes flow cytometry results of BAP1 knockdown effects on death receptor expression and references supporting figure.

claim: 25 human early passage MM lines from the UK Mesobank were assessed for BAP1 expression by immunohistochemistry.
source: 25 human early passage MM lines from the UK Mesobank (Rintoul et al., 2016) were assessed for BAP1 expression by immunohistochemistry, a technique known to correlate strongly with BAP1 LOF mutations in the absence of strong nuclear staining (Nasu et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach for assessing BAP1 status in early passage cultures.

claim: Immunohistochemistry correlates strongly with BAP1 LOF mutations in the absence of strong nuclear staining.
source: 25 human early passage MM lines from the UK Mesobank (Rintoul et al., 2016) were assessed for BAP1 expression by immunohistochemistry, a technique known to correlate strongly with BAP1 LOF mutations in the absence of strong nuclear staining (Nasu et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature establishing the correlation between IHC and BAP1 mutations.

claim: Early passage MM lines without strong nuclear BAP1 staining were significantly more sensitive to rTRAIL than those with strong nuclear staining (p=0.0067).
source: When treated with rTRAIL, those without strong nuclear staining were significantly more sensitive than those with strong nuclear staining (p=0.0067).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical analysis of the association between BAP1 IHC status and TRAIL sensitivity.

claim: Of the 12 early passage MM lines that did not express nuclear BAP1, 9 were sensitive, 2 partially sensitive and only one resistant to rTRAIL.
source: Of the 12 lines that did not express nuclear BAP1 9 were sensitive, 2 partially sensitive and only one resistant to rTRAIL (Table 1, Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on the sensitivity distribution of BAP1-negative early passage cultures and references supporting table and figures.

claim: rTRAIL treatment of tumour explants derived from three patients with MM revealed increased levels of apoptosis in explants with low BAP1 expression compared with those with high BAP1 expression.
source: Remarkably, rTRAIL treatment of tumour explants derived from three patients with MM also revealed increased levels of apoptosis (as measured by poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) cleavage) in explants with low BAP1 expression compared with those with high BAP1 expression (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results from patient tumor explants and references supporting figures.

claim: At sacrifice, rTRAIL-treated BAP1-mutant tumors weighed significantly less than rTRAIL-treated BAP1-wild-type tumors (p=0.020).
source: At sacrifice rTRAIL-treated BAP1-mutant tumours weighed significantly less than rTRAIL-treated BAP1-wild-type tumours (p=0.020) and vehicle-treated BAP1-mutant tumours (p=0.019) (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical analysis of tumor weights from xenograft experiments and references supporting figures.

claim: At sacrifice, rTRAIL-treated BAP1-mutant tumors weighed significantly less than vehicle-treated BAP1-mutant tumors (p=0.019).
source: At sacrifice rTRAIL-treated BAP1-mutant tumours weighed significantly less than rTRAIL-treated BAP1-wild-type tumours (p=0.020) and vehicle-treated BAP1-mutant tumours (p=0.019) (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical analysis of tumor weights from xenograft experiments and references supporting figures.

claim: BAP1-wild-type tumors showed no response to rTRAIL compared with vehicle.
source: BAP1-wild-type tumours showed no response to rTRAIL compared with vehicle.
evidence: The manuscript describes the lack of response in wild-type tumors from xenograft experiments.

claim: The growth rate of rTRAIL-treated BAP1-mutant tumors was significantly suppressed compared with rTRAIL-treated BAP1-wild-type and vehicle-treated tumors (p<0.05) as assessed by longitudinal bioluminescence intensity.
source: The growth rate of rTRAIL-treated BAP1-mutant tumours was also significantly suppressed compared with rTRAIL-treated BAP1-wild-type and vehicle-treated tumours (p<0.05) as assessed by longitudinal bioluminescence intensity (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical analysis of tumor growth rates from xenograft experiments and references supporting figures.

claim: Malignant mesothelioma currently has no biomarker-driven therapies in routine clinical use.
source: Malignant mesothelioma (MM) currently has no biomarker-driven therapies in routine clinical use.
evidence: The manuscript states the current clinical situation for MM treatment.

claim: The mainstay of medical therapy for all MM patients remains systemic cytotoxic chemotherapy that offers only limited survival benefit in unselected populations.
source: The mainstay of medical therapy for all patients remains systemic cytotoxic chemotherapy that offers only limited survival benefit in unselected populations; as such the disease remains invariably fatal (Vogelzang et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature describing the current standard of care and outcomes for MM.

claim: CDKN2A, NF2, BAP1 and TP53 are the most frequently mutated genes in MM.
source: CDKN2A, NF2, BAP1 and TP53 are the most frequently mutated (Guo et al., 2015; Bueno et al., 2016) and there has been increased focus on these genes and their associated signaling pathways as potential therapeutic targets (LaFave et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature identifying the most frequently mutated genes in MM.

claim: rTRAIL and other death receptor agonists selectively induce apoptosis in cancer cells.
source: rTRAIL and other death receptor agonists selectively induce apoptosis in cancer cells and have long held promise as anti-cancer agents owing to their broad clinical utility and minimal off-target effects (Wiley et al., 1995; Pitti et al., 1996; Ashkenazi et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature describing the mechanism and promise of death receptor agonists.

claim: Successful preclinical studies of death receptor agonists have not translated to clinical efficacy in trials of unselected populations.
source: Despite this, successful preclinical studies have not translated to clinical efficacy in trials of unselected populations (Herbst et al., 2010; Wainberg et al., 2013; Soria et al., 2010; Lemke et al., 2014a); there have been no trials to date in MM.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature describing the failure of death receptor agonists in clinical trials.

claim: There have been no trials of death receptor agonists to date in MM.
source: Despite this, successful preclinical studies have not translated to clinical efficacy in trials of unselected populations (Herbst et al., 2010; Wainberg et al., 2013; Soria et al., 2010; Lemke et al., 2014a); there have been no trials to date in MM.
evidence: The manuscript states the absence of clinical trials of death receptor agonists in MM.

claim: BAP1 is a nuclear deubiquitinase and forms multi-protein complexes that regulate the transcription of genes involved in key cellular functions including cell cycle regulation and DNA repair.
source: BAP1 is a nuclear deubiquitinase and forms multi-protein complexes that regulate the transcription of genes involved in key cellular functions including cell cycle regulation and DNA repair (Ismail et al., 2014; Machida et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature describing BAP1 function.

claim: Loss of BAP1 function modulates mRNA and protein expression of components of the extrinsic apoptotic pathway.
source: We further found that loss of BAP1 function modulates mRNA and protein expression of components of the extrinsic apoptotic pathway.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from gene expression and protein analysis experiments.

claim: Next-generation sequencing reveals MM BAP1 mutation rates in the order of 20–30%.
source: While next-generation sequencing reveals MM BAP1 mutation rates in the order of 20–30% (Guo et al., 2015; Bueno et al., 2016; Bott et al., 2011), immunohistochemical analysis has identified loss of BAP1 function in up to 67% of MM tumours (Nasu et al., 2015) opening our biomarker-driven approach to a significant proportion of MM patients.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature reporting BAP1 mutation frequencies in MM.

claim: Immunohistochemical analysis has identified loss of BAP1 function in up to 67% of MM tumors.
source: While next-generation sequencing reveals MM BAP1 mutation rates in the order of 20–30% (Guo et al., 2015; Bueno et al., 2016; Bott et al., 2011), immunohistochemical analysis has identified loss of BAP1 function in up to 67% of MM tumours (Nasu et al., 2015) opening our biomarker-driven approach to a significant proportion of MM patients.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature reporting BAP1 loss by IHC in MM.

claim: BAP1 immunohistochemistry accurately identifies loss of BAP1 function as a consequence of genetic and non-genetic mechanisms.
source: BAP1 immunohistochemistry accurately identifies loss of BAP1 function as a consequence of genetic and non-genetic mechanisms (Nasu et al., 2015) and is already in clinical use as a diagnostic tool; hence the clinical tools for our proposed approach are validated and ready.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature describing the utility of BAP1 IHC.

claim: BAP1 immunohistochemistry is already in clinical use as a diagnostic tool.
source: BAP1 immunohistochemistry accurately identifies loss of BAP1 function as a consequence of genetic and non-genetic mechanisms (Nasu et al., 2015) and is already in clinical use as a diagnostic tool; hence the clinical tools for our proposed approach are validated and ready.
evidence: The manuscript states the current clinical use of BAP1 IHC.

claim: Chromosomal deletions and somatic inactivating mutations in BAP1 have been identified at high frequency in uveal melanoma.
source: Chromosomal deletions and somatic inactivating mutations have been identified at high frequency in uveal melanoma (Harbour et al., 2010), clear cell renal carcinoma (Peña-Llopis et al., 2012) and cholangiocarcinoma (Fujimoto et al., 2015), increasing the potential clinical impact of our discovery.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature reporting BAP1 alterations in uveal melanoma.

claim: Chromosomal deletions and somatic inactivating mutations in BAP1 have been identified at high frequency in clear cell renal carcinoma.
source: Chromosomal deletions and somatic inactivating mutations have been identified at high frequency in uveal melanoma (Harbour et al., 2010), clear cell renal carcinoma (Peña-Llopis et al., 2012) and cholangiocarcinoma (Fujimoto et al., 2015), increasing the potential clinical impact of our discovery.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature reporting BAP1 alterations in clear cell renal carcinoma.

claim: Chromosomal deletions and somatic inactivating mutations in BAP1 have been identified at high frequency in cholangiocarcinoma.
source: Chromosomal deletions and somatic inactivating mutations have been identified at high frequency in uveal melanoma (Harbour et al., 2010), clear cell renal carcinoma (Peña-Llopis et al., 2012) and cholangiocarcinoma (Fujimoto et al., 2015), increasing the potential clinical impact of our discovery.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature reporting BAP1 alterations in cholangiocarcinoma.

claim: Loss of BAP1 function is seen at 1% in breast carcinoma.
source: Although loss of BAP1 function is seen at far lower rates in breast carcinoma (1%) (Stephens et al., 2012) and non-small cell lung carcinoma (1%) (Owen et al., 2017), the high incidence of these cancers translates to a large cohort of patients.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature reporting BAP1 loss frequency in breast carcinoma.

claim: Loss of BAP1 function is seen at 1% in non-small cell lung carcinoma.
source: Although loss of BAP1 function is seen at far lower rates in breast carcinoma (1%) (Stephens et al., 2012) and non-small cell lung carcinoma (1%) (Owen et al., 2017), the high incidence of these cancers translates to a large cohort of patients.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature reporting BAP1 loss frequency in non-small cell lung carcinoma.

claim: Numerous clinically tested death receptor agonist compounds have demonstrated limited therapeutic efficacy at phase I/II trials.
source: Focus on death receptor agonists as anti-cancer agents has generated two decades of preclinical studies and the development of numerous clinically tested compounds, all of which have demonstrated limited therapeutic efficacy at phase I/II trials (Herbst et al., 2010; von Pawel et al., 2014; Paz-Ares et al., 2013; Forero-Torres et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature describing clinical trial outcomes for death receptor agonists.

claim: Within death receptor agonist trials some patients showed signs of therapeutic benefit.
source: However, within these trials some patients showed signs of therapeutic benefit and differential sensitivity within cell lines is well known.
evidence: The manuscript states observations from clinical trials suggesting heterogeneous responses.

claim: Differential sensitivity to death receptor agonists within cell lines is well known.
source: However, within these trials some patients showed signs of therapeutic benefit and differential sensitivity within cell lines is well known.
evidence: The manuscript states established knowledge about variable sensitivity to death receptor agonists.

claim: Retrospective biomarker identification has led to the stratified use of other anti-cancer therapies that initially failed in unselected trials such as activating EGFR mutations and EGFR TKIs.
source: Retrospective biomarker identification has led to the stratified use of other anti-cancer therapies that initially failed in unselected trials such as activating EGFR mutations and EGFR TKIs (Lynch et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature describing the precedent for retrospective biomarker identification.

claim: The BAP1-ASXL1 complex, the Polycomb repressive deubiquitinase (PR-DUB), is key to mediating TRAIL sensitivity.
source: We investigated which BAP1 protein-binding partners, and thus which regulatory complexes, mediate TRAIL sensitivity identifying the BAP1-ASXL1 complex, the Polycomb repressive deubiquitinase (PR-DUB), as key.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from experiments testing different BAP1 mutants and ASXL knockdown.

claim: Loss of BAP1 augments sensitivity to TRAIL in cancer cells.
source: Loss of functional BAP1 augments sensitivity to TRAIL in cancer cells
evidence: This is the title of the manuscript, summarizing the main finding supported by multiple experiments.

claim: BAP1 loss-of-function mutations are frequent in MM.
source: We identify BAP1 loss-of-function mutations, which are frequent in MM, as a potential genomic stratification tool for TRAIL sensitivity with immediate and actionable therapeutic implications.
evidence: The manuscript states the frequency of BAP1 mutations in MM based on cited literature.

claim: BAP1 is a potential genomic stratification tool for TRAIL sensitivity.
source: We identify BAP1 loss-of-function mutations, which are frequent in MM, as a potential genomic stratification tool for TRAIL sensitivity with immediate and actionable therapeutic implications.
evidence: The manuscript proposes BAP1 as a biomarker based on the experimental findings showing association between BAP1 status and TRAIL sensitivity.

claim: Transduction of two further BAP1-mutant rTRAIL-sensitive cell lines, H28 and H2804, with wild-type BAP1 induced resistance to rTRAIL.
source: Transduction of two further BAP1-mutant rTRAIL-sensitive cell lines, H28 and H2804, with wild-type BAP1 also induced resistance to rTRAIL while sensitivity was maintained with transduction of the deubiquitinase mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results of BAP1 rescue experiments in additional cell lines and references supporting figure.

claim: Sensitivity to rTRAIL was maintained in H28 and H2804 cells with transduction of the deubiquitinase mutant BAP1.
source: Transduction of two further BAP1-mutant rTRAIL-sensitive cell lines, H28 and H2804, with wild-type BAP1 also induced resistance to rTRAIL while sensitivity was maintained with transduction of the deubiquitinase mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results showing that the C91A mutant did not rescue TRAIL resistance in these cell lines and references supporting figure.

claim: A marginal trend towards increased sensitivity in BAP1 mutant MM lines in response to treatment with the agonistic FAS receptor antibody CH11 was observed.
source: A marginal trend towards increased sensitivity in BAP1 mutant MM lines in response to treatment with the agonistic FAS receptor antibody CH11 and a TNF-α/IAP inhibitor combination was observed.
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from experiments testing other TNF superfamily agonists.

claim: A marginal trend towards increased sensitivity in BAP1 mutant MM lines in response to treatment with a TNF-α/IAP inhibitor combination was observed.
source: A marginal trend towards increased sensitivity in BAP1 mutant MM lines in response to treatment with the agonistic FAS receptor antibody CH11 and a TNF-α/IAP inhibitor combination was observed.
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from experiments testing other TNF superfamily agonists.

claim: The trend observed with other TNF superfamily agonists indicates the BAP1-rTRAIL association to be mediated by an underlying mechanism common to this family such as the cytoplasmic extrinsic apoptotic machinery.
source: However, this was not as pronounced as that observed with rTRAIL or the multivalent death receptor five superagonist MEDI3039 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D and E). Thus, while the significant sensitising association observed in the screen appears most specific to death receptor agonists, the trend observed with other TNF superfamily agonists indicates the BAP1-rTRAIL association to be mediated by an underlying mechanism common to this family such as the cytoplasmic extrinsic apoptotic machinery.
evidence: The manuscript infers a common mechanism based on the pattern of responses to different TNF superfamily agonists.

claim: Drugs such as tyrosine kinase inhibitors developed against the BCR-ABL fusion product in chronic myeloid leukaemia have transformed the prognosis of these cancers.
source: Drugs such as the tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) developed against the BCR-ABL fusion product in chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) and the receptor products of HER2 mutations in breast cancer have transformed the prognosis of these cancers (Druker et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature describing the impact of targeted therapies in CML.

claim: Drugs such as tyrosine kinase inhibitors developed against the receptor products of HER2 mutations in breast cancer have transformed the prognosis of these cancers.
source: Drugs such as the tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) developed against the BCR-ABL fusion product in chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) and the receptor products of HER2 mutations in breast cancer have transformed the prognosis of these cancers (Druker et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature describing the impact of targeted therapies in breast cancer.
